When I was 13, my family and I all became born again Christians. We joined a little Independent Fundamental Baptist church. Anyone familiar with the denomination knows what that means regarding modesty. Now, IFB churches here in Ontario are often a little less "fundy" than IFB churches in the USA, but still, compared to most other Christian denominations in the country, they're still pretty strict. It took me about a year before I decided to get rid of my shorts and pants and wear only skirts and dresses. I believed it was the only way to be modest because I trusted that the people who told me "the Bible says women need to wear dresses and men need to wear pants" were actually right. Anyway. So after having a few kids in my early 20s, I began to really hate my wardrobe. It was the early 2000s and it was getting harder to find modest skirts and dresses that were still at least somewhat fashionable. Eventually, when I was 26, I sneakily bought my first pair of pants in 12 years at a local thrift shop and packed them into my summer vacation suitcase. Long story short, it was the beginning of the end of my Baptist dressing habits. It was around that time that my husband deconverted from his beliefs and told me he was an atheist. It started a period of serious doubt and questioning for me (something he'd been silently going through for a few years prior, poor guy!), and in time I became resentful and rebellious against the ways we had been taught to believe and live. I got rid of most of my clothes because I felt horrible when I wore them. I started wearing short shorts, snug-fitting spaghetti strap tank tops, and a bikini to the beach. I still never wore dresses or skirts above the knee though; you can't sit down in 'em and I felt exposed. But I knew that what I was wearing showed off my figure well. And that should've been more of a red flag to me than it was. A married lady has no business being a show-off like that.

In my rebellion (ours, I should say; he had some struggles of his own from his past), and in my husband's atheism, we both swung fairly hard left in our social opinions, politics, and in my religious opinions. My clothing was less modest than it should've been, and I made some foolish choices motivated by a pseudo-feminist belief that I should be able to do what I want and not feel shame. I stopped caring about what men thought about what I looked like or how I behaved. But I didn't give enough thought to what just one man who actually mattered to me thought or felt. Our marriage hit a rough patch and it was a time of big change for both of us as we realized that our liberal ideas - and particularly my subsequent behaviour! - had nearly cost us dearly. Especially me. It's sobering to look back and realize that even just toeing that line nearly ruined me. Since then we have both swung back around into conservative values. He is no longer an atheist, though what he is now is hard to explain and is a story for another day.

All that to say, I have been reevaluating my wardrobe over the last year. Last summer, I got rid of my short shorts and replaced them with mid-thigh ones. I need more for this year. This spring, I've been replacing all my spaghetti-strap tank tops with modest sleeveless tops in a looser cut. I will likely still swim in a bikini because I never went for the itsy bitsy string ones; I always choose a full-coverage bottom and a top that keeps the girls very well-covered so as not to suffer a wardrobe malfunction. And it's appropriate at the beach. But I will no longer wear one in front of his half of the family. I'm gonna find a new one-piece for this year's summer vacation.

Modesty for me means "appropriate". I wouldn't wear a bikini to church but it's appropriate on a beach. I try to think about whether an outfit is appropriate to wear given where I'm going and who with. For example, I have a "cold shoulder" blouse - basically off the shoulder but with a thin strap on each shoulder to hold it up. I wear it to rock concerts or date nights with my husband. If I wear it when I'm not with him, I will throw something over my shoulders for coverage. I have some bell-bottom jeans that fit like a glove from the hip to the knee; I only wear them with a long, loose tunic for coverage. I like to balance things that way - I find it keeps an outfit from looking like I'm after attention. If I'm wearing something that is fitted on my bottom half, like a pair of slim-fit jeans, I keep the top loose; fitted on the top half, loose on the bottom. It looks better on me than all loose.
